title: Idioms and Phrases
shortDescription: Fixed expressions whose meaning you cannot guess from the individual words — English's favourite way to set a trap.
genZNote: Do not translate these literally. English loves setting traps with perfectly ordinary-looking words that mean something totally different together.

sections.heading: Why idioms can't be translated word-by-word
sections.body: An idiom is a fixed group of words whose overall meaning is different from the literal meaning of each individual word — 'kick the bucket' has nothing to do with buckets; it means 'to die'. Because idioms are fixed expressions, exams test whether you know the CONVENTIONAL meaning, not whether you can logically deduce it from the words.

rows: To avoid getting to the point
To let the cat out of the bag
To study/work late into the night
To add fuel to the fire
To make a bad situation worse
To hit the nail on the head
To describe exactly what is causing a situation
Something that seems bad but turns out good
To face a difficult situation bravely
To ease tension and start a conversation
To stop working on something for the time being

sections.heading: How to approach idiom questions
bullets: Never answer literally — if an option restates the individual words rather than the conventional meaning, it is almost always the wrong trap answer.
Idioms usually test MEANING recognition (match the idiom to its meaning) rather than requiring you to write the idiom yourself, so focus revision on meanings, not perfect recall of wording.
Group idioms by theme (secrecy, difficulty, happiness, anger, rarity) — this mirrors how they're often tested and makes revision faster.
Regional/contextual variation exists, but competitive exams test the standard, widely accepted meaning — don't overthink alternate readings.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Idioms are fixed expressions with a conventional meaning that cannot be worked out from the literal words, so they must be learned as whole units.
keyFacts: Never interpret an idiom literally — the individual words are a decoy.
Idioms are best revised grouped by theme (secrecy, difficulty, happiness) rather than as a random list.

highYieldFacts: 'Let the cat out of the bag' = reveal a secret; 'once in a blue moon' = very rarely — two of the most commonly tested idioms.
commonTraps: Picking the option that describes the LITERAL scene in the idiom rather than its actual figurative meaning.
mustRemember: If an idiom is unfamiliar, eliminate any answer option that just restates the words literally.
possibleQuestions: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to burn the midnight oil'.
Choose the correct idiom for 'to face a difficult situation with courage'.
